title: Linguistic inequity in academia: evidence from publication patterns in philosophy, 1975–2021
abstract: [Abstract] Linguistic inequity affecting non-native English speakers is widely documented in academia. This inequity is especially visible in philosophy, where success depends unusually heavily on the quality and nuance of written expression. Yet existing studies rely on small samples from a handful of elite journals, limiting their generalizability. We address this gap with the most comprehensive empirical analysis to date, covering 103,595 articles published across 223 journals between 1975 and 2021. Using two automated classifiers based on institutional affiliation and PhD country (accuracy above 89%), we estimate authors’ linguistic backgrounds at scale. We find strong evidence of severe underrepresentation of non-native authors in top philosophy journals across all classifiers, while evidence for underrepresentation in non-top journals is mixed. Moreover, while representation has improved since 1975, progress has been slower in elite journals. We investigate three potential explanations for the gap between high-prestige and non-top journals: language quality, active discrimination, and differences in research interests. We find at best suggestive evidence for the language-quality hypothesis; evidence that the adoption of double-blind review is associated with improved non-native representation (a pattern consistent with active discrimination); and evidence that prestigious journals disproportionately publish in subfields where non-native English speakers are less represented. Taken together, these findings illustrate how linguistic background can shape access to publication opportunities in academia.

title: Artificial intelligence transparency statements and publication governance in medical literature: cross-sectional analysis of 97,916 articles, 2015–2026
Equipping the next generation: addressing the unmet need for artificial intelligence education at research performing organizations
abstract: Background The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools into higher education is rapidly accelerating, yet the educational ecosystem appears largely unprepared for the scale and speed of adoption. Our recent international survey of over 1,200 university students and postdoctoral fellows in the medical and life sciences found that while more than 80% had used GenAI tools, the vast majority had received no formal training, and many were unaware of any institutional policies governing their use. This gap between adoption and institutional preparedness may pose risks to research integrity if left unaddressed. Main body Existing research supports a coordinated, evidence-informed approach to AI education in research performing organizations (RPOs), grounded in principles of research integrity, equity, and critical engagement with technology. First, GenAI literacy must be embedded as a core competency in scientific and clinical education, equipping students to critically evaluate tool outputs, recognize hallucination and bias, and understand the distinction between AI-generated inaccuracy and deliberate research misconduct. Second, traditional frameworks for academic integrity would benefit from re-examination. Today, GenAI tools have fundamentally disrupted established notions of authorship, originality, and plagiarism, and the absence of coherent institutional guidance leaves students and educators navigating these questions without support. Third, RPOs must develop clear, transparent, and context-sensitive policies on GenAI use by embedding responsible AI education into curricula, equipping learners not only to use these tools effectively, but to question, verify, and critique their outputs in ways that uphold scientific standards. Conclusion RPOs have an urgent responsibility to move beyond reactive responses and toward proactive strategies that uphold scientific standards, promote equity of access, and prepare the next generation of researchers and clinicians to engage with GenAI responsibly and ethically.

title: Attitudes and perceptions toward the use of artificial intelligence chatbots for peer review in medical journals: a large-scale, international cross-sectional survey
abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence chatbots (AICs) are increasingly being considered for use in scholarly peer review to assist with tasks such as identifying methodological issues, verifying references, and improving language clarity. However, concerns remain regarding their reliability, ethical implications, and transparency. Evidence on how medical journal peer reviewers perceive the role and impact of AICs is limited. This study explored reviewers’ familiarity with AICs, perceived benefits and challenges, ethical concerns, and anticipated future roles in peer review. MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional online survey of medical journal peer reviewers. Corresponding author information was extracted from MEDLINE-indexed articles added to PubMed within a six-week period. A total of 72,851 authors were invited via email to participate; those who self-identified as peer reviewers were eligible. The 29-item survey assessed familiarity with AICs and perceptions of their benefits and limitations in peer review. The survey was administered via SurveyMonkey from April 28 to June 16, 2025, with two reminder emails sent during the data collection period. ResultsOf 66,679 email invitations, a total of 1260 respondents provided survey responses (response rate: 1.9%), of whom 1157 met the eligibility criteria, and 1077 answered the main survey questions. Most participants were familiar with AICs (86.2%) and had used them for general purposes (87.7%), though most report not using AICs for peer review purposes (70.3%). Most respondents reported that their institutions do not provide training on AIC use in peer review (69.5%), although many expressed interest in such training (60.7%). Perceptions of AIC benefits were mixed, while concerns were widely shared, particularly regarding potential algorithmic bias (80.3%) and issues related to trust and user acceptance (73.3%). ConclusionsWhile familiarity with AICs is high among medical journal peer reviewers, their reported use in peer review remains limited. There is clear interest in training and guidance, however, concerns related to ethics, data privacy, and research integrity persist and should be addressed before broader implementation.

"Can we replicate your findings?" Assessing the availability of reproducibility assets in machine learning-based concrete research
abstract: [Abstract] Research on machine learning (ML)-based concrete property prediction has expanded significantly, yet the availability and accessibility of research assets needed to support independent verification remain insufficiently characterized. This study investigated 419 articles indexed in the Science Citation Index Expanded (SCIE) of the Web of Science Core Collection that were retrieved with the WoS Publication Year filter set to 2025 and focused on tabular data-based ML studies predicting concrete properties from mixture-related variables. The availability and accessibility of datasets, source code, and graphical user interfaces (GUIs) were manually verified and further analyzed by journal quartile and corresponding author country. The empirical findings reveal a profoundly low asset-sharing rate; algorithmic source codes remained undisclosed in 90.7% of the literature. For datasets, full raw data sharing stood at only 21.5%, whereas 50.4% relied on external citations. Furthermore, an analysis of 85 GUI-developed publications showed that 66.0% and 53.6% of instances in Q1 and Q2 journals, respectively, exhibited a developed-but-restricted access pattern. An exploratory review of Data Availability Statements identified several stated reasons for restricting asset sharing, including institutional intellectual property protection and industrial confidentiality agreements, and noted several statements that appeared inconsistent with the data-dependent nature of the reported ML analyses.

title: What AI editing changes in scientific abstracts, and what remains when the AI is asked to sound human
Publishers’ responses to integrity concerns – does the type of notice influence subsequent citations? a cohort study
abstract: [Abstract] [Background] Untrustworthy publications contaminate scientific literature directly through their publication and indirectly by being cited. Journals/Publishers often respond to integrity concerns about publications by publishing an editorial response (editorial notice, expression of concern (EoC) or retraction). We investigated whether the type of editorial response affected citation rates. [Methods] We obtained citations for an index set of 172 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) with integrity concerns (41 received editorial notices, 38 EoCs and 23 were retracted) and control RCTs published in the same journal and year as each index RCT. We calculated monthly citation rates up to 60 months before and after the editorial response and compared them by editorial response type, and to the natural citation decline rate in control RCTs. [Results] 172 index RCTs had 10,603 citations from 6,376 articles. 3,330 matched control trials were identified for 151/172 index RCTs (115,948 citations, 87,811 articles). In the index trials and controls, citations increased steadily, peaking 45–65 months post-publication, then declining. We did not find statistically significant differences in citation decline post-editorial response amongst index trials receiving a retraction, EoC, or notice. Citations were lower in controls than index trials, so analyses were restricted to 1598 highly cited (> 25) controls. The natural rate of decline for highly cited control trials was not statistically significantly different from the post-editorial response rate for all 3 index groups. [Conclusion] We did not find that the decline in citation rates after editorial response publication differed by type of editorial response or from the natural decline in control trials without editorial responses.
